nature-eecon-248.title: Appropriate technology: small, local and affordable
nature-eecon-248.text:
In 1962 E. F. Schumacher described India to its Planning Commission as long in labor and short in capital, and called for technology that used its labor surplus. He first set out the idea as intermediate technology. Appropriate technology is a movement and set of choices that are small-scale, affordable to users, labor-intensive, energy-efficient, environmentally sustainable and locally autonomous.

It is mostly discussed as an alternative to transferring capital-intensive technology from industrialized to developing countries, though the movement exists in both rich and poor ones. Schumacher's idea critiqued development strategies that maximized aggregate growth measured by indicators such as GDP. Imported technology had often produced a two-tier economy benefiting a small urban elite.

The movement grew from 680 organizations listed by the OECD in 1977 to more than 1,000 by 1980, then declined. A 2010 blog post by Paul Polak declared it dead, replaced by design for the other 90 percent. Barriers include its image as a poor person's technology, limited robustness and transferability, insufficient funding and weak institutional support. Open-source appropriate technology, with plans freely available online, marks a resurgence.

nature-eecon-249.title: Consumerism: when buying becomes identity
nature-eecon-249.text:
Around 1900 the average worker still spent 80-90% of income on food and necessities. Consumerism is the socio-cultural and economic phenomenon in which many people aspire to goods and services beyond what is needed for survival or traditional displays. It emerged in Western Europe and the United States during the Industrial Revolution and became widespread around the 20th century. Buying became cultural, social and identity-forming, not only economic. Mass production and mass consumption, exemplified by Henry Ford, were what was needed to propel it.

Critics say consumerist societies damage the environment, contribute to global warming and use resources at a higher rate. Experts link it to the {{ref:nature-eecon-178}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-185}}. Tim Kasser's book argues that people who value wealth and possessions more tend to have lower satisfaction and higher anxiety. Austrian economists object to Keynesian incentives for more consumption, arguing production is what makes consumption possible. Alternatives range from simple living and buying local to freeganism.

nature-eecon-254.title: Simple living: owning, spending and working less
nature-eecon-254.text:
Simple living means owning fewer possessions, using less technology and spending less money. People choose it for spirituality, health, time for family, work-life balance, frugality or environmental sustainability, and it can be a reaction to materialism and consumer culture. Some tie it to degrowth, deep ecology and anti-consumerism goals. Green parties often advocate it.

Spending less means less time earning money. That frees time for other interests, volunteering and quality of life, and lower expenses can bring financial independence. Its roots include Buddhism, Taoism, Epicureanism and Thoreau's Walden (1854). Some adherents increase self-sufficiency through practices such as forest gardening. They differ on technology: neo-Luddites reject it, while others find it makes a simple lifestyle easier, for instance remote work lowering carbon footprints.

nature-eecon-251.title: The second demographic transition
nature-eecon-251.text: In 1986 Lesthaeghe and van de Kaa formulated a framework for changes in sexual and reproductive behavior in North America and Western Europe since about 1963. Cheap, effective contraception, the sexual revolution and women's larger role in work and society produced sub-replacement fertility in industrialized countries. It extends the {{ref:nature-eecon-250}}.

nature-eecon-231.title: Waste: what the holder no longer wants
nature-eecon-231.text:
Waste is unwanted or unusable material, any substance discarded after primary use or judged worthless or defective. What counts as waste varies by viewer. The EU defines it as an object the holder discards, intends to discard or is required to discard. A by-product is a joint product of minor economic value, and an invention that raises a waste product's value above zero can turn it into a by-product, joint product or resource.

Waste is mostly measured by size or weight, which differ: wet organic waste is much heavier, and bottles of equal size can weigh differently. Managing it is costly for municipalities. Pay-as-you-throw policies can cut cost and quantity, and recovery avoids raw material extraction and often cuts transport costs. It is also an environmental justice issue, since burdens fall more often on marginalized groups and residents of developing nations.
